(a) Definitions.—In this section:
        (1) Conservation district.—The term “Conservation District” means the San Bernardino Valley Water Conservation District, a political subdivision of the State of California. 
        (2) Federal exchange parcel.—The term “Federal exchange parcel” means the approximately 90 acres of Federal land administered by the Bureau of Land Management generally depicted as “BLM Equalization Land to SBVWCD” on the Map and is to be conveyed to the Conservation District if necessary to equalize the fair market values of the lands otherwise to be exchanged. 
        (3) Federal land.—The term “Federal land” means the approximately 327 acres of Federal land administered by the Bureau of Land Management generally depicted as “BLM Land to SBVWCD” on the Map. 
        (4) Map.—The term “Map” means the map entitled “Santa Ana River Wash Land Exchange” and dated September 3, 2015. 
        (5) Non-federal exchange parcel.—The term “non-Federal exchange parcel” means the approximately 59 acres of land owned by the Conservation District generally depicted as “SBVWCD Equalization Land” on the Map and is to be conveyed to the United States if necessary to equalize the fair market values of the lands otherwise to be exchanged. 
        (6) Non-federal land.—The term “non-Federal Land” means the approximately 310 acres of land owned by the Conservation District generally depicted as “SBVWCD to BLM” on the Map.  
    (b) Exchange of Land; Equalization of Value.—
        (1) Exchange authorized.—Notwithstanding the land use planning requirements of sections 202, 210, and 211 of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (43 U.S.C. 1712, 1720, 1721), subject to valid existing rights, and conditioned upon any equalization payment necessary under section 206(b) of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (43 U.S.C. 1716(b)), and paragraph (2), as soon as practicable, but not later than 2 years after the date of enactment of this Act, if the Conservation District offers to convey the exchange land to the United States, the Secretary shall—
            (A) convey to the Conservation District all right, title, and interest of the United States in and to the Federal land, and any such portion of the Federal exchange parcel as may be required to equalize the values of the lands exchanged; and 
            (B) accept from the Conservation District a conveyance of all right, title, and interest of the Conservation District in and to the non-Federal land, and any such portion of the non-Federal exchange parcel as may be required to equalize the values of the lands exchanged.  
        (2) Equalization payment.—To the extent an equalization payment is necessary under section 206(b) of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (43 U.S.C. 1716(b)), the amount of such equalization payment shall first be made by way of in-kind transfer of such portion of the Federal exchange 
parcel to the Conservation District, or transfer of such portion of the non-Federal exchange parcel to the United States, as the case may be, as may be necessary to equalize the fair market values of the exchanged properties. The fair market value of the Federal exchange parcel or non-Federal exchange parcel, as the case may be, shall be credited against any required equalization payment. To the extent such credit is not sufficient to offset the entire amount of equalization payment so indicated, any remaining amount of equalization payment shall be treated as follows:
            (A) If the equalization payment is to equalize values by which the Federal land exceeds the non-Federal land and the credited value of the non-Federal exchange parcel, Conservation District may make the equalization payment to the United States, notwithstanding any limitation regarding the amount of the equalization payment under section 206(b) of the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (43 U.S.C. 1716(b)). In the event Conservation District opts not to make the indicated equalization payment, the exchange shall not proceed. 
            (B) If the equalization payment is to equalize values by which the non-Federal land exceeds the Federal land and the credited value of the Federal exchange parcel, the Secretary shall order the exchange without requirement of any additional equalization payment by the United States to the Conservation District.  
        (3) Appraisals.—
            (A) The value of the land to be exchanged under this section shall be determined by appraisals conducted by one or more independent and qualified appraisers. 
            (B) The appraisals shall be conducted in accordance with nationally recognized appraisal standards, including, as appropriate, the Uniform Appraisal Standards for Federal Land Acquisitions and the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice.  
        (4) Title approval.—Title to the land to be exchanged under this section shall be in a format acceptable to the Secretary and the Conservation District. 
        (5) Map and legal descriptions.—As soon as practicable after the date of enactment of this Act, the Secretary shall finalize a map and legal descriptions of all land to be conveyed under this section. The Secretary may correct any minor errors in the map or in the legal descriptions. The map and legal descriptions shall be on file and available for public inspection in appropriate offices of the Bureau of Land Management. 
        (6) Costs of conveyance.—As a condition of conveyance, any costs related to the conveyance under this section shall be paid by the Conservation District.  
    (c) Applicable Law.—
        (1) Act of february 20, 1909.—
            (A) The Act of February 20, 1909 (35 Stat. 641), shall not apply to the Federal land and any public exchange land transferred under this section. 
            (B) The exchange of lands under this section shall be subject to continuing rights of the Conservation District under the Act of February 20, 1909 (35 Stat. 641), on the non-Federal land and any exchanged portion of the 
non-Federal exchange parcel for the continued use, maintenance, operation, construction, or relocation of, or expansion of, groundwater recharge facilities on the non-Federal land, to accommodate groundwater recharge of the Bunker Hill Basin to the extent that such activities are not in conflict with any Habitat Conservation Plan or Habitat Management Plan under which such non-Federal land or non-Federal exchange parcel may be held or managed.  
        (2) FLPMA.—Except as otherwise provided in this section, the Federal Land Policy and Management Act of 1976 (43 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.), shall apply to the exchange of land under this section.  
    (d) Cancellation of Secretarial Order 241.—Secretarial Order 241, dated November 11, 1929 (withdrawing a portion of the Federal land for an unconstructed transmission line), is terminated and the withdrawal thereby effected is revoked.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that the Conservation District (a local government body), the independent appraisers, and the map's "public inspection" bring outsiders into a federal decision. But the section directs a land-exchange transaction in which the District is a counterparty offering and accepting property, not a party consulted on a federal policy decision. The appraisers perform a technical valuation, and making a map available for inspection is disclosure only. There is no comment period, hearing, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue.

opus.w: This section authorizes a land exchange with a local water district. The District's involvement (offering its land, choosing whether to pay to equalize values, agreeing on title) is that of a party to a property deal, not consultation on a federal policy decision. The tempting reading treats the District's approval of title, the independent appraisals, or public inspection of the map as participation. But these are terms of a transaction, valuation inputs, and passive disclosure, with no comment period, hearing, advisory body, rulemaking, or right to sue.
opus.s: Title to the land to be exchanged under this section shall be in a format acceptable to the Secretary and the Conservation District.
opus.b:
I labelled this **No**. It is a negotiated land swap between the federal government and a local water district, and nothing in it brings outsiders into a federal policy decision.

**The tempting reading.** The San Bernardino Valley Water Conservation District is a local political subdivision, so it is outside the federal government. Several provisions also look like outside involvement:
- The exchange happens only "if the Conservation District offers" to convey its land.
- The District can decide not to make an equalization payment, which stops the exchange.
- Title must be "acceptable to the Secretary and the Conservation District."
- Independent appraisers set the land values.
- The map is available "for public inspection."

**Why it fails.** The District takes part as the other party to a property deal, not as a consultee or adviser. Its offer, its payment choice and its approval of title are a counterparty's terms, which is closer to the contracts and applications the definition excludes. The appraisers supply valuations, much like the outside financial experts in Example 3, who informed a study rather than a decision. Public inspection of a finished map gives no chance to comment, and there is no hearing, advisory body, rulemaking or right to sue.

The closest call is the mutual title-approval clause. Because it is a real outside sign-off on part of the deal, I'm only moderately confident.

qwen_chat.w: The section describes a specific land exchange between the federal government and a local conservation district. While it requires independent appraisers, this is a transactional requirement to determine value for a specific deal, not a participatory process where outside parties advise on or influence a broader federal policy decision. The definition excludes applications for benefits or grants, and this land swap is analogous to a specific administrative transaction rather than a rulemaking or advisory process. The mention of public inspection of maps is passive and does not constitute consultation or coordination before a decision.
qwen_chat.s: (3) Appraisals.— (A) The value of the land to be exchanged under this section shall be determined by appraisals conducted by one or more independent and qualified appraisers.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for "independent and qualified appraisers" constitutes participation because these are outside experts. However, the definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits or grants, and this section is primarily about a specific land exchange transaction. The appraisers are hired to determine value for a specific transaction, not to advise on a general policy decision or rulemaking. Furthermore, the "public inspection" of maps is passive access to information, not active consultation or coordination before a decision is made. The core interaction is a bilateral agreement between the federal government and a specific local entity (the Conservation District) to swap land, which is a transactional matter rather than a participatory decision-making process involving the general public or advisory bodies.
